items.title: News Analysis: Krakow shooting shakes Poland's sense of security
text: By Xinhua writers Yue Yuanyuan, Guo Shunag
WARSAW, Nov. 8 (Xinhua) -- Gunfire shattered a Saturday afternoon in Krakow's historic market square, leaving a country where mass shootings are rare confronting an unfamiliar fear.
As Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday, prosecutors opened an investigation, treating the shooting as a terrorist offense, which left six people dead and 16 injured.

Coming barely a month after three school stabbings in four days, the attack has deepened concerns about young people turning to extreme violence. Although no link between the cases has been established, Poland faces a broader challenge: how to prevent further attacks and restore a shaken sense of security.

The gunman in the Saturday afternoon mass shooting was identified by police as a 24-year-old Polish citizen, who held a firearms licence and had no previous criminal record. He was wounded in an exchange of fire with police officers.

The National Prosecutor's Office said the suspect was believed to have killed six people and attempted to kill others, including police officers, in the market square. He was also suspected of killing three members of his family at their home in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski.
The three victims found dead at the family home were identified as the parents and sister.

The shooting has shocked a country with a comparatively strong record on several measures of public safety. According to an earlier estimate by the Geneva-based Small Arms Survey, Poland has 2.5 civilian-held firearms per 100 people, the lowest rate in the European Union.

Separately, an analysis of Eurostat's 2023 survey data by the Poland News found that 2.8 percent of people in Poland reported crime, violence or vandalism in their neighborhoods, the third-lowest proportion in the bloc.

These figures help explain the public shock. The contrast between Poland's reputation for relative safety and the devastating consequences of the attack has raised questions about how to prevent such incidents.

The Krakow shooting has brought renewed attention to radicalization among young people, as the suspects in three school stabbings in October that left one person dead and several wounded were 15, 19 and 21, respectively.
Although no link between the cases has been established, official statements have drawn attention to the possible influence of online violent content and extremist ideas.

After the school attacks, Prime Minister Donald Tusk pointed to the glorification of violence online and warned of imitation. Authorities also reported increased interest in Nazi material and mass killers who had acquired an online following.
One 15-year-old suspect had worn a helmet-mounted camera and intended to film his attack, Tusk said.

In the Krakow case, investigators are examining a possible ideological motive. Polish Minister of Internal Affairs and Administration Marcin Kierwinski said preliminary information suggested the suspect held highly radical views and may have been fascinated by far-right ideologies.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

Taizhou pupils build circuits at electrical safety workshop
text: State Grid Taizhou Power Supply Company recently held a workshop at Huaqiao Town Central Primary School in Sanmen county, Zhejiang province, as part of the "Power Love Classroom" volunteer program. The workshop combined a lesson on electrical safety with a hands-on circuit-building exercise for students at the rural school.

At the event, model workers, skilled artisans and young volunteers served as guest instructors. Drawing on examples from home and school, they explained how electricity is generated and used in daily life. The lesson also covered how to use electricity safely, save energy, stay safe during thunderstorms and respond to an electric shock.

The instructors used animations and examples to illustrate common unsafe practices involving electricity. Students took part in a question-and-answer session and discussed the hazards shown in the examples, along with ways to use electricity safely at home and at school.

After the lesson, volunteers provided students with batteries, wires, bulbs, switches and other materials for an experiment. They explained the basic principles of series and parallel circuits, then guided the students step by step through the process of connecting the components.

The students tested the circuits they had assembled and used them to light up small bulbs. By working with the components themselves, they put the principles covered in the lesson into practice and saw how the parts of a circuit work together to power a bulb.

The company plans to expand its volunteer activities under the "Power Love Classroom" program. It will continue to offer regular lessons on electricity and electrical safety for young people in rural schools and communities.

items.title: FM: China willing to buy more Papua New Guinea LNG
text: On Monday, China said it welcomed Papua New Guinea's decision to close Taiwan's so-called representative office and was willing to import more liquefied natural gas from the Pacific nation, after the Taiwan region said it would sign no new spot contracts for the fuel.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said the PNG government's decision once again showed that upholding the one-China principle is where international public opinion trends and the arc of history bends.

"China appreciates this and will continue working with PNG to firmly support each other's core interests and major concerns," Guo said in response to a question raised after Monday's regular news briefing.

Guo said China stands ready to increase imports of liquefied natural gas from PNG, deepen cooperation in economy, trade, and other areas, and add new dimensions to their comprehensive strategic partnership.

Taiwan's so-called "foreign affairs office" announced the closure of the "Taipei Economic Office" in Port Moresby, capital of PNG, on Friday, and said that "no new spot contracts" for purchasing liquefied natural gas will be signed with the Pacific nation.

items.title: Book explores Fu culture from global perspective
text: The Chinese and English editions of Fu Culture: A Global Perspective, a book focused on exploring the diversity and coexistence of Fu culture from a global perspective, were launched at a symposium in Beijing on Thursday.
The event brought together officials, scholars, cultural experts, international guests and media representatives.

"The research seeks to identify shared values across cultural and civilizational differences, using the universal pursuit of happiness as a basis for greater understanding and consensus," said Li Mi, a professor at Beijing International Studies University and author of the book.

In his remarks, Chang Bo, the president of China International Communications Group, said the traditional Chinese Fu culture could contribute to cross-cultural dialogue and a broader understanding of human well-being.

Ruan Shiwei, president of the Association for Yan Huang Culture of Fujian, said, "Some academic publications on Fu culture focus excessively on auspicious patterns, folk traditions, and cultural customs, narrowing the meaning of Fu culture and making it appear as though it is merely a superficial decorative element unique to Chinese culture. Others tend to interpret and reconstruct Fu culture through Western cultural perspectives and intellectual frameworks. As a result, the original roots and essence of Chinese Fu culture are weakened."

Rafael Zerbetto, an expert from China International Communications Group, who has been living in China for over 10 years and won the Chinese Government Friendship Award in 2025, said he had learned that "you cannot understand a culture unless you allow it to change you".

He added, "This book invites us into a genuine cultural dialogue in which we are not merely observing, but willing to be transformed by the encounter. And that is the true meaning of Fu in a global perspective. It is about recognizing that happiness is a shared human destination, and that every culture brings its own unique wisdom to the journey."

The discussion also touched on the implications of artificial intelligence for the pursuit of happiness. Zheng Chengjun, vice-president of Beijing International Studies University, said the emergence of AI was changing the ways people experience and pursue happiness. He described Fu as the pursuit of a better life, a better world and a more fulfilling human existence, saying that exploring how to promote goodness in the development and application of AI could become an important direction for future research.

items.title: Gilead showcases liver disease advances at 9th CIIE
text: Gilead Sciences showcased a range of innovative treatments and initiatives in liver disease at the 9th China International Import Expo in Shanghai, highlighting its efforts to address unmet medical needs ranging from viral hepatitis to rare liver conditions as it seeks to expand access to therapies in China.

The US drugmaker presented treatments for hepatitis B and C alongside seladelpar, a first-in-class oral treatment for primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), a rare chronic liver disease. It also highlighted progress in clinical access, standardized diagnosis and treatment, and partnerships with healthcare institutions and other organizations.

A key focus was seladelpar, whose application for marketing approval in China is under review by the National Medical Products Administration. The treatment, marketed as Livdelzi in the United States, received accelerated approval from the US Food and Drug Administration in August 2024 for adults with PBC who have an inadequate response to ursodeoxycholic acid, or cannot tolerate it.

First showcased at the CIIE in 2024, seladelpar was subsequently made available to eligible patients through special access programs in Beijing and Hainan province in 2025, Gilead said. The treatment has also been included in overseas specialty drug lists under supplementary commercial health insurance plans in Beijing, Hainan, Jinan in Shandong province, and the cities of Suzhou and Nanjing in Jiangsu province.

PBC is a chronic autoimmune liver disease that mainly affects women and can cause persistent itching and fatigue. Without effective treatment, it can progress to cirrhosis or liver failure. The disease was included in China's second national list of rare diseases in 2023.

On Nov 5, Gilead reported positive results from its Phase 3 IDEAL trial of seladelpar. Among 96 adults with PBC enrolled in the study, 75.4 percent of those receiving seladelpar met the primary endpoint after 52 weeks, compared with 16.1 percent in the placebo group.
The endpoint was a composite measure requiring alkaline phosphatase, or ALP, a marker of disease activity, to reach the normal range and decline by at least 15 percent from baseline.

The trial focused on patients whose ALP levels remained above normal but below 1.67 times the upper limit of normal despite treatment with ursodeoxycholic acid for 12 months, or who could not tolerate the medicine. Gilead said the results would be discussed with regulatory authorities globally and that no new safety concerns had emerged.

"Over five consecutive years of participating in the CIIE, several of our innovative therapies have moved from exhibition displays into clinical use," said Jin Fangqian, vice-president and China general manager of Gilead Sciences.

From viral hepatitis to rare liver diseases, Gilead said it would continue working with government bodies, healthcare institutions and patient organizations to improve disease awareness, promote standardized care and expand access to innovative treatments in China.

items.title: China's factory-gate inflation surges amid higher global energy prices
text: China's factory-gate inflation climbed to a nearly four-and-a-half-year high in October as global energy prices rose, while consumer price growth remained modest, data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed on Monday.

The producer price index, which tracks factory-gate prices, rose 5.7 percent year-on-year in October, up from 5 percent in September, the bureau said. It was the fastest increase since June 2022, when producer prices rose 6.1 percent, according to the bureau's data.
On a month-on-month basis, producer prices rose 0.7 percent in October, down from a 1.2 percent gain in September.

Six energy-related industries, including oil and gas extraction and petroleum refining, accounted for more than 80 percent of the increase, said Dong Lijuan, a statistician at the bureau, citing higher global energy prices and stronger fuel demand ahead of winter.
"Progress in managing industrial capacity and rapid advances in artificial intelligence also lifted prices in parts of the raw materials and equipment manufacturing sectors," Dong added.

Meanwhile, the consumer price index, a key gauge of inflation, rose 0.7 percent year-on-year in October, compared with 0.9 percent in September. Gasoline prices climbed 22.4 percent from a year earlier, contributing about 0.63 percentage points to CPI growth, the bureau said.

Lower food prices helped temper consumer price growth in October, with its year-on-year decline widening by 1.2 percentage points to 2.9 percent. Prices for fresh vegetables, pork and fresh fruit fell 16.9 percent, 8.6 percent and 3.8 percent, respectively, lowering the year-on-year CPI increase by about 0.54 percentage points, the bureau said.
The CPI remained unchanged month-on-month in October after rising 0.2 percent in September, the bureau said.

Core CPI — which excludes food and energy prices and offers a clearer gauge of underlying price pressures — rose 0.8 percent year-on-year in October, easing from a 1 percent increase in September, the bureau added.

items.title: Living libraries: A possible step out of the social bubble
text: Why are Chinese youth so quick to grasp a concept and put it into action on a scale a European could only dream of? How do they nurture so much synergy that even a two-day exchange can take root and become a successful practice from Day 1? Would a generation that finds paper books obsolete and reading slow favor the idea of giving libraries a new perspective by borrowing humans instead of books to learn their life stories?

These questions have filled my mind since I volunteered at an exchange activity on the Living Library methodology, which was hosted by the Guangdong Association for STD and AIDS Prevention and Control and led by a close friend and colleague, together with students from the Not Awkward Youth Club, an outstanding student volunteer group.

Fifty students from various majors and universities, backed by an excellent team of facilitators, worked like a well-balanced organism, bursting with energy and positive spirit, learning and implementing on the spot.

Ten years ago, we came up with the idea of using Forum Theatre for HIV and sexual abuse prevention. After three consecutive exchange activities under the China-Europe NGO Twinning Programme, Forum Theatre is now performed in front of more than 50,000 people a year at more than 700 events, with thousands of videos on social media and youth platforms. Many young people are familiar with the concept of replaying a performance together with the audience in order to find a solution. And they actively apply it. It is amazing!

This year, the idea was to show young people how to host a "living library" event in their local communities, where the "books" are real people from all walks of life and the "readers" are encouraged to ask open-minded questions in order to learn more about their experiences and build empathy and social understanding. The goal is to step out of our small circle of friends and colleagues and talk with people we would not normally meet, and to combat the alienation of social media and screen time and replace it with kind and curious human-to-human dialogue, especially given the challenges AI will bring.

Did they achieve it? Absolutely! At the end of the activity, six young people volunteered as librarians and hosted an event with eight "books" and many readers. I, a Bulgarian teacher and youth worker, without understanding a single word of Chinese, stood there in awe, convinced that from now on the "living library" will be one of the many successful and inspiring methods of promoting social dialogue in China.
The author is a Bulgarian ESL teacher working in Guangzhou.
The views don't necessarily reflect those of China Daily.

text: 【财新网】近日，北京京剧院发布讣告，著名京剧艺术家、一级导演迟金声先生仙逝，享年104岁。在京剧界，寿逾百岁者并不多见，而且，他是民国京剧大师马连良先生亲传弟子中，去世最晚的一个。然而，综其一生，这位马连良闭门弟子对京剧的贡献，并非台前亮相，而在于幕后耕耘，凡数十年而不辍，且与时偕行，可称一代梨园功臣。

1922年，迟金声出生于古老的戏曲世家。迟家第一代名迟宝财，又名迟财官，其具体生卒年月已不可考，只知道他是活跃于清乾嘉时期的京腔武生演员，名列“京腔十三绝”之一，还曾任精忠庙首（即后来的梨园公会会长，为旧时北京戏曲界的最大行会组织）。需要注意的是，这里所说的京腔并非京剧，而是经北京语音改造的弋阳腔。弋阳腔是与昆曲同样古老的高腔戏曲，以武戏见长，在清乾嘉时代是北京颇为流行的戏种，故名京腔。“京腔十三绝”也远早于后来京剧的“同光十三绝”，因为彼时京剧尚未形成，其前身徽调也未在京流行。所以，作为戏曲世家，迟家远早于我们熟知的京剧世家，如谭家、梅家和叶家。到了迟家第三代迟春祥，已是四大徽班之一三庆班的著名武老生演员，自此，迟家进入开始繁盛的京剧行，几代绵延、名家辈出。曾在电视连续剧《西游记》中饰演唐僧、后与女富豪陈丽华结婚的迟重瑞也是同族后人，此前也是京剧演员。

items.title: More Chinese Regions to Require Autumn and Spring School Breaks
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019236/More Chinese Regions to Require Autumn and Spring School Breaks
text: More Chinese regions are implementing autumn and spring breaks in compulsory education, expanding a decadelong national initiative. Some have also waived fees for students on break and rolled out support measures to help parents take leave at the same time as their children.

Spring and autumn holidays across all compulsory education schools have been rolled out provincewide in at least 15 provinces, as well as numerous cities in other provinces, such as the southern megacity of Shenzhen, domestic media reported last week. In China, compulsory education lasts nine years, encompassing primary and middle school. Breaks will occur in November and April for four to five days each.

The reform dates back to 2004, when Hangzhou, capital of the eastern province of Zhejiang, piloted the breaks. In 2013, the initiative expanded nationally when the State Council issued an announcement encouraging local governments to adopt it, and the rollout accelerated again in 2025 when central authorities urged more schools to implement the holidays.
Chu Zhaohui, a researcher at the China National Academy of Educational Sciences, told domestic media outlet Red Star News that the holidays actually boost learning.
“Learning isn’t confined to schools or taught only by teachers and parents,” Chu said, adding that the holidays give students space for self-exploration.

At the same time as introducing spring and autumn holiday policies, many cities have also added supporting measures so parents can sync their leave. In October, Longnan city in the northwestern Gansu province encouraged employers to implement paid leave and prioritize compensatory rest for employees with school-age children, aligning staff leave with school holidays.

Foshan, a city in the southern Guangdong province, also issued a proposal on Nov. 3 calling on employers to prioritize arranging leave for employees with children during the autumn holiday. The city’s five-day autumn break begins Nov. 11.

Many tourist spots are also waiving entrance fees for children during the upcoming fall break. In the eastern city of Wuxi, a theme park dropped entry fees for students 16 and under throughout November; 15 top tourism sites in Huangshan in the eastern Anhui province, a city known for its mountain of the same name, are now entry-free for children under 18; and the Dujiangyan scenic area in the southwestern Sichuan province waived fees for primary and middle school students between Nov. 12 and 16.

The breaks have significantly boosted travel demand, according to online travel booking platform Qunar. Data from Qunar revealed that in November, air ticket bookings for children 12 and under increased 1.6 times year on year, while parent bookings rose by 50%.

Wang Qiyan, director of the Leisure Economy Research Center at Renmin University, told Red Star News that spring and autumn breaks “enable off-peak travel, avoiding the packed scenic spots of winter and summer vacations.

items.title: A Bad Review, a Suicide, and a Debate Over Cyberbullying in China
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019228/A Bad Review, a Suicide, and a Debate Over Cyberbullying in China
text: On Oct. 6, 2026, a female customer posted complaints on multiple social media platforms about a fried skewer stall in Gao County, Yibin, in southwestern China’s Sichuan province. “Avoid XX Copper Pot Potatoes. The owner can’t take the heat,” she wrote. She had bought a 10-yuan ($1.40) fried food combo from the stall, run by a 33-year-old woman surnamed Hu, but was dissatisfied with the portion of potatoes. “She just refused to add potatoes afterward,” the customer added. Her location-tagged posts quickly spread, and negative comments about Hu and her stall flooded the comment sections.
Hu responded to the criticism, writing, “I stand behind my portions.” Three days later, on Oct. 9, she jumped into a river and died by suicide.

Hu had run the stall for more than four years, sleeping less than six hours a night. In her suicide note, she described the enormous pressures she faced in life. She had hoped to watch her child grow up, she wrote, but the video telling people to avoid her stall had been the straw that broke the camel’s back.

She also wrote: “These past two days I have experienced what I consider cyberbullying. One person complained about no potatoes in her order, and then the comments came flooding in about bad service and poor-tasting food.”

This was not the first tragedy of its kind. In August 2025, a 57-year-old obstetrician-gynecologist surnamed Shao in Zhoukou, central China’s Henan province, jumped to her death. According to her family, she had endured more than seven months of cyberbullying over a medical dispute. In 2023, after a primary school student in Wuhan, capital of the central Hubei province, was killed in a traffic accident on campus, his mother was subjected to online attacks and later jumped to her death. In cases like these, public opinion often attributes the tragedies to cyberbullying.
But in Hu’s case, labeling the entire incident “cyberbullying” and placing the blame on the customer who posted the negative review would exaggerate the power of a single act of expression.

The customer maintained that she was simply describing a genuine experience, with “no malice, incitement, or falsehood.” She did not insult or personally attack anyone, disclose private information, or call for coordinated attacks online or offline. Her criticism may have been harsh, subjective, or exaggerated, but based on the content of her posts alone, it is difficult to characterize it as cyberbullying.

Many negative comments about the stall owner appeared beneath the posts, but there is currently no evidence that they were all malicious. Public criticism can be harsh, but legal liability must rest on provable facts.

In July 2026, China released a draft Anti-Online Violence Law for public comment. It defines online violence as “concentrated or sustained” acts involving “insult and abuse, rumor-mongering and defamation, incitement of hatred,” and similar behavior. A negative review based on a genuine transaction cannot automatically be classified as cyberbullying because it has harmful consequences. Moreover, the draft has not yet become law.

items.title: China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019225/China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting
text: As it expands its weather-warning systems across the Global South, China has handed over equipment for a customized version of MAZU — an AI-powered weather prediction tool created by the China Meteorological Administration — to Sri Lanka, one of eight countries where the platform has been deployed.

The device, described by domestic media as a rectangular black box roughly the size of a portable toolbox, was presented to Sri Lanka’s meteorological department on Nov. 1. It will form part of a system designed to warn of heavy rain, strong winds, and cyclones, and is expected to enter service by the end of the year.

Launched in July 2025, MAZU takes its name from a Chinese sea goddess revered as a protector of sailors. It combines AI forecasting models developed by Chinese research institutions with data from the country’s weather satellites.
Conventional weather forecasting relies on supercomputers to calculate how the atmosphere will change using equations based on physical laws. AI models, by contrast, learn from years of weather data.

“Chatbots familiar to the public learn patterns in language, while AI weather models learn how the atmosphere evolves,” Niu Zeyi, an assistant researcher at the Shanghai Typhoon Institute who led the development of a forecasting model used in MAZU, told Sixth Tone. “By training on years of meteorological data, these models can predict future weather conditions based on current variables such as wind, air pressure, temperature, and humidity.”

Once trained, AI models can produce forecasts faster and more cheaply than conventional methods. One model can generate a 24-hour global forecast in 1.4 seconds, about 10,000 times faster than traditional numerical methods. For forecasts covering 15 to 60 days, AI models can reduce computing costs to one-thousandth of those of conventional methods.

But most of the savings come from running routine forecasts, Niu said. Training models, building datasets, and maintaining systems still require investment — resources many countries in the Global South lack.
MAZU’s cloud-based services are being tested by 58 countries, according to domestic media, and China plans to deploy the system in 30 countries over the next five years.

In Pakistan, the system has reportedly incorporated local radar and satellite data to develop warnings for heavy rainfall and glacial lake outburst floods. In Djibouti, the model developed by Niu’s team helps provide tailored weather warnings for the East African country’s port.

Studies show AI models can be less accurate than conventional methods when predicting record-breaking extremes, for which there is little historical data. Local weather in complex terrain also remains difficult to forecast, and it is not always clear how AI models arrive at their predictions.

The models also need to be adapted to local conditions, Niu said. “Our approach is to work with local meteorological agencies to improve datasets, conduct independent evaluations, and make local adjustments.”
Even with AI, he added, “human forecasters must still combine observations, AI predictions, and their own judgment before authorities issue warnings.”

items.title: China’s Traditional Colors Are Trending. But What Are We Missing?
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019218/China’s Traditional Colors Are Trending. But What Are We Missing?
text: Traditional Chinese colors have become a popular topic on Chinese social media, with posts sporting catchy headlines such as “Our Ancestors Had the Ultimate Eye for Beauty” and “Out-of-This-World Color Combinations in ‘Dream of the Red Chamber.’” Open one of these posts, and you’ll often find neatly arranged color swatches labeled with evocative traditional names such as tianqing, “celestial blue”; yuebai, “moon white”; qiuxiang, “autumn fragrance”; and yanzhi, “rouge.”

In my opinion, this enthusiasm is undoubtedly a good thing. Traditional colors deserve greater attention and should be made more accessible. Color swatches can also be useful for showcasing the colors of historical artifacts and help modern audiences connect with the past. But this kind of simplification is a double-edged sword. In making something rich and complex easier to understand, it can also reduce it to a crude, one-dimensional representation. What makes information easier to communicate can also obscure or distort its meaning.
In fact, color swatches have significant limitations when it comes to representing and explaining traditional colors. They can only scratch the surface of a much richer cultural history.

Modern color charts emerged from Western industrial and commercial systems designed to control production quality and reproduce specific colors. But this standardized, scientific approach often falls short when applied to traditional Chinese colors. Anyone who has visited an exhibition of antique clothing or textiles and tried to photograph it may have experienced this firsthand. What appears to the naked eye as a beautiful pine green might look mustard yellow on a smartphone screen. Or the various golds and yellows of an imperial dragon robe might lose their distinctiveness entirely. If even digital cameras equipped with sophisticated image-processing algorithms struggle to capture these colors, what chance does a simple color swatch have?
So why do modern industrial color charts fall short in representing traditional Chinese colors?

First, color swatches are designed to standardize colors within specific product categories, whereas traditional Chinese color names developed within particular craft traditions. As these traditions evolved, a color’s name could refer to subtly different hues in different periods.

Several factors contributed to these variations. In the age of traditional handicrafts, differences in materials and craftsmanship could produce markedly different hues. Local production conditions also gave products from different regions their own distinctive characteristics. Fashions changed over time, altering the shades associated with particular color names. Even on a single garment, colors could appear different depending on the lighting, viewing angle, or direction of the weave.

Traditional indigo dyeing offers a good example. Indigo must first be fermented in vats and chemically reduced before it can be used to dye fabric. A single dip produces a pale blue, and the color deepens after each subsequent immersion. As a result, even fabrics dyed in the same vat can emerge in countless different shades.

items.title: China Vows to Share Its Market With the World at 9th Annual CIIE
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019224/China Vows to Share Its Market With the World at 9th Annual CIIE
text: Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang pledged to share China’s market with the rest of the world and promote balanced international economic development at the opening ceremony of the 2026 China International Import Expo (CIIE) on Thursday.
“Mutual benefit is at the heart of trade and economic cooperation,” Ding said in his opening address. “Open and connected markets are fundamental for such partnerships.”
Ding also called for deeper investment cooperation, greater collaboration in technological innovation, and stronger dialogue to remove trade barriers.

This year’s CIIE, the ninth annual event and the largest edition to date, welcomes a record 4,142 overseas companies from 162 countries, regions, and international organizations to Shanghai’s National Exhibition and Convention Center. The event’s total exhibition area is also its largest, exceeding 440,000 square meters.

The event, which runs Nov. 5 to 10, welcomed more than 300 Fortune Global 500 companies and global leading enterprises, with 2,000 companies participating for the first time. A record more than 480 products will either make their global, Asia, or China debut at the expo, including a laparoscopic surgery robot by Johnson & Johnson, a cochlear implant capable of 360-degree sound coverage by Swiss hearing care firm Advanced Bionics, and a 6G terminal prototype by U.S. tech company Qualcomm.

This year’s exhibition comprises six main sections covering technical equipment, consumer goods, food and agricultural products, automobiles and smart mobility, medical devices and health care, and trade in services. It also offers a dedicated “innovation incubation zone” for tech startups.

CIIE has also expanded efforts to support African countries, with free exhibition booth space for the “least developed” countries up 17% from last year’s exhibition. The expansion comes as China introduced zero tariffs on imports from all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations in May.

Launched in 2018, CIIE is the world’s first national-level exhibition dedicated to imports. The expo underlines China’s continued efforts to promote inclusive economic globalization and build an open world economy.
In the first nine months of 2026, China’s imports of foreign goods reached 16.7 trillion yuan ($2.5 trillion), up 22.3% year on year, the fastest growth since 2021, according to official data.
(Header image: A view of the China International Import Expo’s exhibition center in Shanghai, Nov. 5, 2026. VCG)

items.title: Double 11 Looming, Chinese Shoppers Ask Strangers to Vet Their Carts
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019220/Double 11 Looming, Chinese Shoppers Ask Strangers to Vet Their Carts
text: Applications aimed at preventing impulse purchases have soared in popularity during this year’s Double Eleven, the world’s largest shopping festival. The apps involve users listing the items they want, along with their prices, then sharing them with friends and strangers who vote on whether they should buy them.

Dozens of such mini-programs have sprung up across major platforms including WeChat and Alipay following the August success of the WeChat mini-program “Still Want to Buy?” (Hai Mai Me in Chinese), domestic media reported last week. Related hashtags have garnered tens of millions of views on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, as of Thursday.

Domestic e-commerce giant Alibaba launched Double Eleven, also known as Singles’ Day, on Nov. 11, 2009, as a 24-hour shopping event. The festival has since grown to a monthlong event across all e-commerce platforms and begins around mid-October.

The trend comes as young Chinese consumers become increasingly money-conscious. According to a May report by Ireland-based consulting firm Accenture, 82% of the country’s Gen Z — more than 230 million people — have started saving money or cutting back on non-essential spending.

The rise in anti-impulse-buy apps dates back to the release of Still Want to Buy? in August. Created by a 29-year-old developer under the pseudonym Qiancheng, the app gained more than 75,000 daily active users within three days of its launch, and total registered users exceeded 500,000 as of mid-September. More than 85% of users are females under 24, Qiancheng told local media.

He said the tool came about after his girlfriend suggested using automated office purchase approval systems — which employees must go through to obtain authorization for work-related purchases — to govern shopping decisions. He added that he often personally feels regret after making impulse purchases.
“It’s difficult to make money nowadays, so I think it’s worth letting people we trust help us make better spending decisions,” Qiancheng said.

However, Still Want to Buy? was taken down on Oct. 31, reportedly due to targeted reporting from online trolls. Qiancheng told local media he is applying to have the mini-program relisted and is developing an independent app to expand the program’s function.
WeChat mini-program “Wait Up, Wallet” also offers similar features to Still Want to Buy?, but it allows users to seek advice from total strangers.

This October, Lin Yinjie, a 20-year-old college student from the eastern Fujian province, vibe-coded a similar app, the Alipay mini-program “Hold On a Sec.” The app lets users log items and prices and set a cooling-off period, during which friends help them decide whether to buy. So far, the program is mainly used by Lin and her friends and does not have a wide audience.

Lin told Sixth Tone that she used to place orders mindlessly while scrolling shopping apps and social media. “As a student on a tight budget, I know how easily the desire to buy things can quietly drain my wallet,” she said.

items.title: Record number of product debuts at CIIE highlights China’s emerging role as innovation hub
text: "Show China your best." That is the invitation the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) extends to the world. The response? More than 480 products and technologies making their global, Asian or China debuts, from 6G device prototypes and AI computing systems to innovative medicines, luxury skincare and fragrances - a vibrant showcase of global innovation meeting the energy of China's vast consumer market that is more open to new products and ideas.

For global companies, the CIIE is more than a showcase for new products. It is a window into China - one that opens onto a vast consumer market, an evolving innovation landscape and expanding opportunities for international cooperation. What comes through that window is not just a flow of goods, but a deeper exchange of ideas, technologies and opportunities.

At Qualcomm's booth in the Technology and Equipment Exhibition Area, visitors are lining up to see what the US chipmaker describes as the world's first 6G device prototype compliant with the latest 3GPP specifications. Making its global debut at the expo, the prototype is among the booth's main attractions.

Another new arrival is the large-model-native agent phone STEPX Neo, which integrates applications and services including Alipay, Jianying (CapCut) and Trip.com. Its combination of hardware, software and AI models points to how AI agents could become more closely integrated into everyday mobile services.

Intel is taking a different approach to the AI boom, focusing on where computing power is generated and how it is supplied. Its CIIE debut is a computing solution that places computing clusters inside shipping containers, with flexible energy storage modules, allowing them to operate closer to renewable energy sources.

"Rather than bringing electricity to computing centers, it makes more sense to move computing clusters closer to where the electricity is generated," Intel China Chairman Wang Zhicong told the Global Times.
The solution, first conceived as an idea at last year's expo, combines computing power, renewable energy and storage, with Chinese energy and IT companies involved in its development.

The exhibits are not confined to technology and equipment. In healthcare, Roche is presenting nearly 100 debut and first-show exhibits, including innovative medicines for breast cancer, lupus nephritis and other diseases. Boehringer Ingelheim is showcasing 14 innovative pipeline products and solutions in human pharmaceuticals and animal health, with three therapies at the forefront of global R&D making their China debut.

Both companies are also looking to deepen their engagement with China's medical innovation ecosystem. Vivian Bian, CEO of Roche Pharma China, told the Global Times that Roche will take the CIIE as an important fulcrum for open cooperation, continue to increase its local investment, and deeply integrate into China's medical innovation ecosystem.

items.title: Annual CIIE opens in Shanghai, showcasing China's commitment to opening up
text: On Thursday morning, in the waiting lounge of the opening ceremony of the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai, two hours before the ceremony began, the guests had already begun arriving.

They took selfies, chatted, posed for group photos with old friends and gave interviews to the media. According to on-site observations by the Global Times, in the relaxing atmosphere, the words they mentioned most were "opportunity", "openness" and "market."

Running from Thursday to Tuesday next week, this year's CIIE has attracted 4,142 overseas exhibitors, with total exhibition area exceeding 440,000 square meters. Over 480 exhibits are set to make their global, Asian or China debut at the event, the highest number in history. In addition, nearly 200 companies and institutions have been "full attendees" at the CIIE for all nine editions.

In his keynote speech at the opening ceremony, Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang, also a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, said that the CIIE has witnessed China's firm determination and concrete actions to promote high-standard opening-up, the remarkable results and tremendous gains of businesses and people from various countries in sharing opportunities in the Chinese market, and the unremitting efforts and important contributions of visionary people from all walks of life in improving global economic governance, according to Xinhua News Agency.

This fully demonstrates China's strategic resolve in advancing high-standard opening-up, injecting valuable certainty, stability and confidence in development into the world, Hu Qimu, professor at the Maritime Silk Road Institute of Huaqiao University, told the Global Times on Thursday.

Gabonese President Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema, Federal Chancellor Christian Stocker of Austria, and UN Development Programme Administrator Alexander De Croo attended the opening ceremony and delivered remarks, Xinhua reported.

Ding's speech was welcomed by many executives from global multinational companies, who said they draw great inspiration from the speech and remain confident in honoring their long-term commitment to China.

Rogier Janssens, President of Merck China, told the Global Times that CIIE brings the world to China, and gives China a stronger voice in the global conversation. "As China moves into its 15th Five-Year Plan, the Expo's role is even more important," Janssens said.

The CIIE opening ceremony underscored the importance of openness, collaboration and innovation-driven development, further reinforcing Henkel's confidence in the long-term growth of the Chinese market, Anna An, President of Henkel China told the Global Times on Thursday.

Vice Premier Ding's speech reaffirmed China's steadfast commitment to high-standard opening-up and highlighted the country's important role in driving growth and building an open global economy, echoed Poh-Yian Koh, President of FedEx China.

items.title: Recalibrating the world's cognitive coordinates
text: In September 2026, the Global South moved to recalibrate the world's old cognitive coordinate system at three levels: institutions, initiatives and public discourse.

At the institutional level, on Sept. 4, the UN General Assembly adopted a resolution on "correcting the map" by a vote of 164 to 1, encouraging the replacement of the Mercator projection, which inflates high latitudes and compresses the equator, with the Equal Earth projection. The United States cast the sole opposing vote.

At the level of initiatives, on Sept. 12-13, BRICS leaders issued a declaration in New Delhi explicitly calling for international law and international rules to be "applied equally, without double standards."

At the level of public discourse, from Sept. 22 to 28, the General Debate of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly was held at UN Headquarters in New York. From Nairobi to Belgrade, leaders took turns criticizing the same thing: international law is being applied selectively.

From the projection of a map to the scale on which a rule is applied and then the authority to interpret an order, the domains differ and the levels differ, but the question being asked was the same: Who sets the world's cognitive coordinates?

This recalibration first took place on the map. The Mercator projection was born in the Age of Exploration as a technical tool for ocean navigation. It accurately represents direction and routes, but systematically distorts area.

Over the centuries, the navigation chart made its way into textbooks and newspaper pages, and eventually became what people took to be "the world itself." A technical choice originally made for navigation thus quietly became the default framework through which people perceived the world.

In this projection, the higher the latitude, the more it is magnified. Europe and North America accordingly sit at the top of the map, while regions in the equatorial belt, such as Africa and Latin America, are compressed. Greenland looks nearly as big as Africa on the map, yet Africa's actual land area is 14 times the size of Greenland.
The African Union notes that the world's long-standing perception of Africa rests on a distorted map. The UN General Assembly resolution therefore means far more than a technical fix to map-making.

It does not require the Mercator projection to withdraw from navigation and aviation, nor should it. What it challenges is the monopoly of the "default base map": When public communication needs to show the true size and position of countries, it cannot continue to present a base map that magnifies the few and compresses the many as if it were the world as it actually is.

At the same time, correcting a bias is not about replacing one bias with another, such as drawing a map that elevates the South, but about acknowledging that every projection involves trade-offs. The question is which set of trade-offs has been treated as the only standard.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: 2026 World Ocean Week spotlights China's ocean governance role
text: The 2026 World Ocean Week opened on November 5 in Xiamen, southeast China's Fujian Province, unveiling five outcomes, including a publication on seamounts and a dedicated ecological and environmental data product.

The week also features 33 activities, including seminars on marine science and ecology and industry and business matchmaking events, to advance global ocean governance and the high-quality development of the blue economy.

A bilingual report on the status, role and prospects of the Agreement under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement), and China's role in it, was released on the same day.

Compiled by the China Institute for Marine Development Strategy under the Ministry of Natural Resources, the report outlines the significance of the agreement's entry into force and China's contributions to its negotiation and implementation.

The BBNJ Agreement took effect on January 17, 2026, becoming the third implementing agreement to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and filling a legal gap in the conservation and governance of marine biodiversity in areas beyond national jurisdiction.

China participated in nearly 20 years of negotiations and put forward proposals on the agreement's four key areas. Its contributions included promoting a benefit-sharing mechanism for marine genetic resources, advancing area-based management tools, improving transparency in environmental impact assessments and helping developing countries build capacity to implement the agreement.

China has designated marine ecological conservation redlines covering about 150,000 square kilometers, established 353 marine protected areas and carried out 194 marine ecological conservation projects. It is also one of the few countries worldwide to have recorded a net increase in mangrove area.

China has made manned deep-sea submersibles Jiaolong and Fendouzhe, as well as research vessels such as Deep Sea No. 1, available for international scientific expeditions. It preserves nearly 60,000 marine microbial resources and provides international users with access to samples and data.

Under the United Nations Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development, China has led 10 major international science programs, including one on the digital discovery of typical deep-sea habitats.

China has improved its legal framework for environmental impact assessments of activities in the international seabed area, while contractors engaged in mineral exploration there have actively fulfilled their assessment obligations.
Its experience, environmental data, expertise, and trained personnel can help developing countries assess deep-sea activities and promote a greener, low-carbon approach to ocean activities.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: Computing-Electricity Index offers a precise portrait of China's computing power industry
text: Staff members from State Grid Hangzhou Power Supply Company visited China Mobile (Hangzhou) Information Technology Co., Ltd. on November 2, delivering a customized computing operations monitoring report built on a Computing-Electricity Index system. Based on the company's electricity consumption, the team also conducted on-site load analysis, energy efficiency assessment and electricity-use advisory services.

The report covers data center cabinet load rates, server rack deployment rates, green electricity consumption, and rack energy efficiency, offering a clear picture of a company's computing operations and electricity use.

Like a dedicated "health checkup report," it provides a reference for companies to assess the performance of their computing operations, optimize operations and management, and develop expansion plans.

"The Computing-Electricity Index shows that our intelligent computing business is growing rapidly and demand for high-end computing is strong. It recommends that newly added computing capacity be prioritized for intelligent computing and AI inference scenariosputing capacity be prioritized for intelligent computing and A" said the head of the company's data center.

The Computing-Electricity Index uses big power data as its foundation to quantify and score the prosperity of the computing power industry across four dimensions: scale momentum, business climate, expected vitality and green efficiency. The index system consists of two scale-momentum indicators, three business-climate indicators, two future-vitality indicators and two green-efficiency indicators. It can support the government in coordinating computing and power resources, while also providing a basis for enterprises to expand computing capacity, save energy and reduce carbon emissions.

Guided by the index's monitoring results, State Grid Hangzhou Power Supply Company is extending its power services beyond support for individual projects to serve the development of the computing power industry, taking a more proactive approach to service delivery.

Given computing power enterprises' large electricity capacity requirements, rapid load growth and high requirements for power supply reliability, the company has strengthened load monitoring and trend analysis for computing centers, promptly detecting abnormal load fluctuations and providing early warnings on risks related to energy efficiency and power quality.

For key computing projects, it implements list-based management and forms "1+N" service teams to provide contracted power connection services and customized power supply plans, while delivering targeted power supply support based on each enterprise's electricity-use sensitivity level.

items.title: Nvidia Opens Investigation Into Jensen Huang’s Relationship With Suspected Chinese Spy
Nvidia opens investigation after CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy
text: Nvidia Announces Investigation Into CEO Over Ties to Chinese Spy02:09Get more news on   Share Add NBC News to GoogleNov. 8, 2026, 3:33 PM EST / Updated Nov. 9, 2026, 8:05 AM ESTBy Steve Kopack and Dan De LuceNvidia’s board of directors said Sunday that it is opening an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.

The announcement followed recent reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who the newspapers reported had been recruited to spy for China. The two are not related.
A person familiar with the matter told NBC News late Sunday that U.S. intelligence agencies had determined that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and had a relationship with Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.

“The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort,” the company said in a statement.

“A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.”
The company added that while it “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”
In a memo to Nvidia employees that the company shared with NBC News, Huang said: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.”

The New York Times and the Financial Times reported that Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen whose Singapore-based company was buying Nvidia’s advanced chips, had been under surveillance by U.S. intelligence agencies. Those agencies, the reports said, found that she had been recruited to spy by China’s top intelligence agency.
Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that “the so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China.”

Jensen Huang and Nvidia, for years, have been at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom. Nvidia’s products are the most highly sought-after chips in the world; however its top-tier products are mostly restricted from being sold to customers in China because of national security fears.
China has long sought to become a global leader in AI. President Xi Jinping set a 2030 deadline to surpass the capabilities of American AI systems.

Huang, 63, essentially serves as an ambassador for the industry, regularly appearing alongside the likes of President Donald Trump and King Charles III of Great Britain and at conferences to tout his company and what he says will be immense payoff in the future from AI.

items.title: China dismisses as a smear campaign claims of a spy plot involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
Why is Nvidia’s Jensen Huang at the centre of a US-China spy scandal?
text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is facing questions over allegations that a Chinese businesswoman with whom he had a romantic relationship was gathering intelligence for Beijing.

Huang – who cofounded Nvidia, the world’s second-most valuable company after Apple, more than three decades ago – admitted on Sunday to being unfaithful to his wife, but the company said it has no reason to believe United States national security or confidential information has been compromised.

Nevertheless, Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation into whether the 63-year-old Taiwan-US dual national had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation after media reports linking him to Alice Huang, a former executive at a Singapore-based data centre company.
“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” it said in a statement, adding that Jensen Huang fully backs the review.

After the revelations, Nvidia – whose market capitalisation of $4.5 trillion is higher than the gross domestic product (GDP) of Japan, the world’s fourth-largest economy – saw its stock price tumble by more than 4 percent in trading overnight into Monday.

The controversy erupted as Washington seeks to prevent China from obtaining advanced American semiconductors, including Nvidia’s most powerful artificial intelligence chips, as the US and China fiercely compete for AI supremacy.
So what do we know about the affair, and how will this impact US-China relations and the race for AI dominance?

The allegations first emerged in a New York Times investigation late last month, which reported that US intelligence officials believed Alice Huang had been recruited by Beijing to gather information about Nvidia’s chief executive and potentially influence the company’s chip sales to China.

However, the precise nature of the information she allegedly obtained, whether any sensitive material was passed to Beijing and how much Jensen Huang knew about the alleged operation remain unclear. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are not related despite sharing a last name.
The two were reportedly seen together at industry events, including a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang in Taipei during the Computex technology exhibition in 2025.
On Sunday, the Nvidia chief acknowledged his infidelity in a staff memo.
“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” he said.
However, in late October, Jensen Huang had told Bloomberg News that his interactions with Alice Huang were related to her company, Megaspeed, describing them as “completely normal and not unusual”.
Also known as Huang Le, Alice Huang is a Chinese citizen and former senior executive at Megaspeed International, which provides computing infrastructure used to operate and train AI systems.
According to The New York Times, Megaspeed had become one of Nvidia’s largest buyers, purchasing about $4.8bn in equipment from the US firm.

items.title: China Hits Back After Claims Of Plot To Ensnare Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
Alice Huang, Suspected China Spy, Spent Years in Nvidia’s Orbit
See how China finally slowed its ballooning emissions right down
text: The growth of China's emissions may have virtually stopped as it races ahead with its rapid rollout of renewables. Five charts show how it reached this milestone and what lies ahead.

China – the world's largest emitter of carbon dioxide (CO2) – has reached a major milestone: in the first half of 2026, less than half of the country's electricity was generated by coal for the first time in its history.
Twenty years ago, these dirty black rocks were the pillar of China's economy: coal power accounted for 80% of all the electricity the country gobbled as it undertook rapid modernisation.
But while the country's overall electricity demand has expanded since then, growing solar and wind power are increasingly lessening its reliance on coal power.

The result of this substantial shift is a potent signal for the country's – and the world's – effort to reach net zero: the growth of China's CO2 emissions has virtually stopped in recent years, according to one assessment. China's emissions may even have peaked in 2025, according to another analysis – five years ahead of the country's own deadline.

From solar megafarms to electric trucks, here are five charts which tell the story behind China's great emissions slowdown, how it reached this milestone and what lies ahead as it races to reach its target of net zero by 2060.
China's economy has seen monumental growth over the past three decades. So have its CO2 emissions, which ballooned nearly fivefold from 1990 to 2024.
China's global share of CO2 also jumped from around 10% to more than 30% during this period, the largest global increase.

China plays a "pivotal role" in the world's fight against climate change not only because it is the largest CO2 emitter, but also because its emissions have grown at the fastest rate, says Yu Aiqun, a research analyst at Global Energy Monitor (GEM), a non-profit in the US.
"Once China's carbon emissions peak, global carbon emissions will likely peak, too," she says.

Some believe the watershed moment is already upon China. The country's carbon emissions reached their highest level in 2024 and fell in 2025, according to data from Climate Action Tracker (CAT), a collaborative project that assesses governments' climate actions. CAT predicts China's carbon emissions will decrease by about 18% by 2035.

A separate analysis by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish think tank, found that China's CO2 emissions have remained flat or falling since March 2024, bar a small rise in early 2026.

Similar trends have happened before, for example when China's government downsized steelmaking and coal power between 2014 and 2016, and during Covid-19, when lockdowns paused manufacturing and transport activity.

But this time there is a fundamental difference, says Belinda Schäpe, CREA's China team lead. The rapid decline is not only driven by the shrinking output of some heavy industries, but also by China's "enormous expansion" of clean energy and growing use of electricity – instead of fossil fuels – to power machines, vehicles and devices.

items.title: What to Know About the China Spy Allegations Involving Nvidia’s Jensen Huang

Nvidia stock falls 5% as scrutiny turns to Jensen Huang’s relationship with alleged Chinese spy
text: Nvidia shares were down 5% in premarket trading Monday after the tech giant launched an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy.
U.S. intelligence agencies said Alice Huang, an executive at cloud company MegaSpeed, has been passing information to Beijing, according to reports in The New York Times and The Financial Times.
Nvidia said its board has launched an independent investigation following the reports that Huang was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort."
Huang "fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it," the company said in a Sunday statement.
The co-founder and CEO told staff in an email that he had "fallen short" of his responsibility to serve his colleagues, the board, partners and shareholders around the world.
"I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," Huang said in the email.
China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday the "so-called Chinese spy narrative" was unsubstantiated, Reuters reported.
Nvidia was last trading down 5.2% in premarket trading.
The probe has sparked questions about Huang's future as CEO of the company.
But any talk of replacing Huang is "comedy," Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe."
While the probe and affair is a "game changer" for the CEO and company, it doesn't alter the view that Nvidia remains two to three years ahead of China in AI chips, Ives said.

"You're talking about what I would view as a torchbearer — the leader of AI technology — not just in the U.S. but globally. So I think the fact that we're in this situation, from an investor perspective, the clear worry is, does Jensen stay on as CEO? The Street would say probably likely, but given the board investigation, anything could happen, and that creates a huge uncertainty."
Tech stocks took a hammering last week as investors reassessed the data center build-out after Democrats won control of Congress.

Asian tech stocks rose across the region on Monday, rebounding from Friday's losses. Shares of U.S. chipmakers were slightly lower in premarket trading, with Intel, Marvell, Qualcomm and Arm all down over 1%.
Joachim Klement, investment strategist at Panmure Liberum, said the impact is currently contained to Nvidia.

But if Huang's position is "endangered," then "Nvidia might cut back on supporting other companies, whether it's in Asia or in the U.S., that might then spread a little bit more into the other semiconductor names," he said.
U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday praised Huang's leadership but said he hadn't spoken to the CEO about the investigation.
"I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it," the president told reporters.
"He's done an amazing job for our country," Trump added.
Shaun Maguire, partner at Sequoia, also defended the tech giant CEO, saying in a post on X that Huang is "one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation."
He added: "two mistakes don't make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America's AI leadership."
